planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; Red Champion blooms most heavily with steady bright indirect light and consistent warmth.

directions: Red Champion carries a saturated, true fire-engine-red spathe with a high-gloss, waxy finish set off by a slender pale yellow-green spadix, a bolder and more intense red than the pink tones of Pink Champion in the same breeding series. Glossy, deep green, heart-shaped leaves form a compact clumping rosette, and the plant blooms nearly continuously under good indoor conditions, with individual spathes lasting many weeks as cut flowers or on the plant. Pot in a loose, orchid-bark-based mix rather than dense potting soil, keep humidity above 50 percent, and feed lightly during the growing season to sustain repeat bloom. Remove spent spathes at the base to keep the plant tidy and encourage new flower stalks.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; White Champion holds its clean white color best out of direct hot sun.

directions: White Champion produces a crisp, pure white, waxy spathe with only a faint green blush at the base, paired with a pale yellow-green spadix, giving a clean, minimalist look distinct from the pink and red tones of other Champion-series cultivars. Foliage is glossy, deep green, and heart-shaped on a compact, clumping plant that fits easily on a bright windowsill or shaded patio table. Its pure white color makes it a favorite for wedding and event floral work as well as a long-blooming houseplant. Feed lightly through the growing season, keep humidity elevated, and remove spent spathes at the base to encourage continued flowering.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; Livium is a reliable, near-continuous bloomer under stable indoor conditions.

directions: Livium's spathe is pink overlaid with irregular white streaking and speckling, a broken bicolor pattern quite different from the solid pink of Pink Champion or the solid red and white of the other Champion cultivars. Lush, dark green, glossy, heart-shaped leaves frame long-lasting flower stems that are produced nearly year-round in the right conditions, with individual blooms holding their color for up to several months. It is a relatively newer flamingo-flower introduction favored for its unusual painterly spathe pattern in mixed houseplant collections. Keep humidity above 50 percent, water only when the mix begins to dry, and feed lightly during active growth to sustain repeat flowering.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; Midori lacks the anthocyanin pigments of red and pink cultivars, so its color is unaffected by light-driven pigment shifts.

directions: Midori is grown entirely for its spathe, which emerges pale green and matures to a rich, waxy lime green with a matching green spadix, lacking the red or pink pigmentation found in Champion-series and Livium cultivars entirely. The near-monochrome green flower reads as sculptural and modern rather than showy, making it popular in contemporary floral design and foliage-forward houseplant collections. Leaves are the same glossy, deep green, heart-shaped form typical of the species. Keep it in a loose, chunky epiphytic mix, maintain humidity above 50 percent, and feed lightly during the growing season to sustain steady flowering.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; Deco Chocolate's unusual bronze-brown color is prized in specialty cut-flower arrangements.

directions: Deco Chocolate stands apart from the red, pink, white, and green flamingo-flower cultivars with a deep, glossy, reddish-brown 'chocolate' spathe, an unusual bronzed color achieved through selective breeding rather than a simple color shift of a red parent. The spadix is typically a contrasting pale cream, heightening the effect of the earthy spathe tone. Foliage is the same glossy, deep green, heart-shaped form typical of the species, and the plant blooms repeatedly through the year given consistent warmth and humidity. Grow in a loose, chunky epiphytic mix, keep humidity elevated, and feed lightly during the growing season to sustain color and repeat bloom.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix; Zizou's long spadix makes it a distinctive cut-flower selection.

directions: Zizou bears a pink-to-purple-pink spathe paired with a notably long, slender, bright yellow spadix that curves outward well beyond the spathe edge, a more pronounced and elongated spadix than seen on Champion-series or Livium cultivars. Glossy, deep green, heart-shaped leaves form a compact clumping plant typical of the species. The elongated spadix gives cut stems a distinctive, slightly exotic look prized by florists working with mixed tropical arrangements. Grow in a loose, chunky epiphytic mix, maintain humidity above 50 percent, and feed lightly during active growth to sustain repeat flowering.

planting.note: Pot into a small container with well-drained mix in bright, indirect light; Natasja is a compact, naturally dwarf weeping fig cultivar widely trained as indoor bonsai.

directions: Natasja stays noticeably smaller and denser than plain weeping fig, typically holding to about two feet tall as a container plant, with small, glossy, dark green leaves on fine, gracefully weeping twigs. Its tight branching and small leaf size make it one of the most popular benjamina selections for indoor bonsai training, since it backbuds readily after pruning and tolerates the light wiring bonsai styling requires. It is somewhat more compact and slower growing than Too Little but shares that cultivar's dwarf habit. Keep in bright, indirect light with consistent watering and location, since weeping figs of all kinds drop leaves readily after sudden change.

planting.note: Grow as an interior tree or patio specimen in bright, indirect light; Monique is a smaller-statured benjamina cultivar noted for holding its leaves better than most through routine indoor stress.

directions: Monique carries narrow, deep green leaves with a distinctive rippled, wavy margin instead of the smooth edge typical of the species, giving the canopy a slightly ruffled texture. It stays a smaller, more restrained size than standard weeping fig cultivars like Danielle, and is noted as being comparatively less prone to the sudden leaf drop that plagues benjamina after relocation or light changes. Place in the brightest indirect light available and keep watering, temperature, and location consistent to minimize stress. Prune to shape any time of year, since Monique responds well to pinching and tolerates standard or braided-trunk training.

planting.note: Grow as an interior tree or patio specimen in bright, indirect light; Midnight is an especially leaf-drop-resistant weeping fig cultivar well suited to beginners.

directions: Midnight arose as a sport of the Exotica cultivar and carries exceptionally dark, almost blackish-green glossy leaves, noticeably darker than the light green foliage of its Exotica parent or the mid-green tone of the plain species. It is regarded as one of the most leaf-drop-resistant weeping fig selections, making it more forgiving of the light and location changes that typically stress this species. Growth habit is upright with gracefully arching branches similar to other full-sized benjamina cultivars. Keep watering and placement consistent, provide the brightest indirect light available, and avoid cold drafts to keep this already-resilient cultivar looking its best.

planting.note: Grow as an interior tree or patio specimen in bright, indirect light; Exotica's pronounced weeping form makes it a classic choice for a graceful indoor accent tree.

directions: Exotica is distinguished by light green leaves that are notably longer and narrower than the species, with a length-to-width ratio exceeding 3:1, and by a pronounced pendulous, weeping branch habit that is evident even on young plants rather than developing only with age. It is the parent selection behind several later sports, including the darker-leaved Midnight cultivar. The narrow, twisting leaves and cascading branch structure give it a softer, more textured silhouette than broader-leaved cultivars like Danielle. Provide the brightest indirect light available, keep watering and placement stable, and avoid drafts and sudden relocation, which readily trigger leaf drop in this species.

planting.note: Site in bright, indirect light to preserve variegation; Safari needs brighter light than solid-green benjamina cultivars to keep its speckled pattern from fading.

directions: Safari carries dark green, boat-shaped leaves densely speckled and marbled with creamy white flecking, a mottled 'camouflage' pattern quite different from the clean cream-margined edges of Golden King or the near-solid white overlay of Starlight. The curved, cupped leaf shape adds further texture distinct from the flatter foliage of most other benjamina cultivars. Because the pale speckled tissue does less photosynthetic work, it needs brighter indirect light than solid-green cultivars to hold its pattern and avoid reverting toward green. Keep watering consistent, prune out any all-green reversion growth promptly, and protect from cold drafts, which trigger leaf drop in this species.

planting.note: Site in bright, indirect light to preserve variegation; Naomi Gold needs brighter light than solid-green benjamina cultivars to keep its gold feathering from fading.

directions: Naomi Gold has smaller, elliptic to ovate leaves with an acuminate tip and a gently undulating margin, feathered with gold-to-cream variegation over a medium green base rather than the crisper white margins seen on Golden King or Starlight. The soft, feathered blending of gold and green gives it a warmer overall color than other variegated benjamina cultivars. It grows a bit more slowly than solid green selections because of its reduced chlorophyll content. Provide bright, indirect light, keep watering consistent, and prune out any branches that revert to solid green to preserve the variegated pattern.

planting.note: Grow as an interior specimen in bright, indirect light; Baroque's curled leaves give it a sculptural silhouette prized as a specimen accent.

directions: Baroque, sometimes sold as the Curly Weeping Fig, produces medium-sized leaves that curl into a loose tube along the central vein instead of lying flat, a distinctly sculptural, twisted leaf form unlike any other benjamina cultivar in this collection. The glossy, saturated dark green color and rounded, curled outline give the whole plant an unusual, almost ornamental texture that reads more like a novelty accent than a typical weeping fig. It is often grown and sold at a smaller, more compact scale than full-size benjamina cultivars. Place in bright, indirect light, keep watering and location stable, and avoid cold drafts, which cause leaf drop as in other benjamina selections.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Variegata holds its cream leaf pattern best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun.

directions: Variegata is the older, classic variegated rubber tree selection, with broad, glossy leaves showing irregular creamy-white blotches and margins over a green base and only a light pink flush on new growth, a subtler pink tone than the heavily pink-flushed Ruby and a less finely marbled pattern than the gray-green marbling of Tineke. This selection predates both of those newer cultivars and has been grown as a houseplant for decades, giving it a more informal, blotched variegation rather than a uniformly marbled look. Provide bright, indirect light to hold the pattern, since low light causes reversion toward solid green. Wipe dust from the broad leaves periodically, let the top inch or two of mix dry between waterings, and prune out any all-green reversion shoots.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Doescheri is a more delicate, slower cultivar than Ruby or Tineke and can be harder to source.

directions: Doescheri carries leaves noticeably narrower than the broad blades of Ruby or Tineke, patterned in a mottled, camouflage-like mix of gray-green, cream, and pale yellow with a distinctive pink midrib, petiole, and stem. This narrower leaf shape and more delicate, patchy variegation set it apart from the broad-leaved, heavily pink-flushed Ruby and the marbled but wide-leaved Tineke. It is generally a slower, more finicky grower than either of those cultivars and is considered a specialty rather than a mass-market rubber tree selection. Provide bright, indirect light to maintain the pattern, let the top inch of mix dry before watering, and shield from cold drafts and direct hot sun.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10-12; Suncoast stays much shorter than the standard species, making it a good fit for smaller rooms.

directions: Suncoast produces the same large, leathery, deeply veined, violin-shaped leaves as the standard fiddle-leaf fig, but on a much shorter, bushier, more densely branched plant that typically tops out around three to four feet, noticeably more compact than either the species or the taller-growing Compacta selection. Its dense, multi-branching habit forms a full, rounded canopy rather than the tall single-trunk form typical of standard fiddle-leaf fig. Clean the large leaves periodically with a damp cloth to keep them glossy, rotate the pot occasionally for even growth, and avoid cold drafts and sudden relocation, both of which can trigger leaf drop.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10-12; Little Sunshine keeps a narrow, upright profile that suits tight corners better than bushier compact selections.

directions: Little Sunshine carries the same violin-shaped, heavily veined leaves as the species but at a noticeably smaller scale, growing in an upright, architectural form rather than the dense, many-branched bushiness of the Bambino cultivar. Its narrower profile makes it a good fit for a bright corner or narrow floor space where a full-size fiddle-leaf fig or a wide, bushy dwarf selection would not fit as neatly. Growth stays slow and upright without heavy pruning required to maintain shape. Water when the top two inches of soil have dried, avoid cold drafts and sudden relocation, and wipe the leaves periodically to keep them glossy and dust-free.
